info.name: Porto Bus API (local)
info.description:
Every endpoint of the local Porto Bus API, plus the error cases.

## Before you start
Run the API with `make dev` (it listens on http://127.0.0.1:8000).

## Variables
- `baseUrl` – where the API is running
- `stopCode` – default `CMO` (CARMO)
- `line` – default `300`
- `directionId` – `0` or `1`
- `serviceId` – **captured automatically**, see below
- `today` – set to today's date on every request by a collection-level script

## About serviceId
The two `schedule` endpoints need a GTFS `service_id` such as
`DOM|FERIADO:FLUXO 3.1 20260718`. It changes with the timetable, and it is matched
exactly upstream, so typing it by hand is error-prone.

You don't have to: run **Lines → Get services for a line** (or **Stops → Get services
at a stop**) once, and its test script stores today's active service into the
`serviceId` collection variable. Every schedule request then just works.

Running the whole collection top-to-bottom does this for you — the services requests
come before the schedule ones on purpose.

## Two data sources
Requests are labelled by where the data comes from: **GTFS** (the official static
feed) or **live** (stcp.pt's own JSON API). `departures` is the only one that merges
both.

request.description:
Two lists, because upstream returns two:

- `routes` — the lines at this stop, **no direction info**, and only a coarse family colour (`#187EC2` for nearly every city line).
- `directions` — the same lines *with* `direction_id`, `direction_name` and `trip_headsign`.

A line appears in `directions` once per stop, with the direction that actually serves it, so looking up direction by line id is unambiguous.

request.description:
Which GTFS calendars (`service_id`) apply at this stop — e.g. weekday, Saturday, Sunday/holiday.

**Heads-up:** the `monday`…`sunday` flags come back all-zero from upstream for every service. That's their bug, not ours — use `is_active_today`, which is correct.

This request stores the active service into the `serviceId` variable.

request.description: Same as above but for an explicit date. Swap `{{today}}` for e.g. `2026-12-25` to see the holiday calendar.

**The one that matters for a UI.** "When's my bus" for one line at one stop.

Live arrivals for the near term, the timetable for everything after, in one list sorted by time. Every entry is tagged `source: "realtime" | "scheduled"` so a frontend can render a live pill differently from a faded scheduled time.

Duplicates are removed using `delay_minutes`: a bus estimated 18:43 running 5 late *is* the 18:38 slot, so the scheduled 18:38 is dropped rather than shown alongside it.

Direction and colour are detected automatically; `service_id` defaults to today's active one.

The departure board for a location: everything you can still catch on foot, ordered by arrival.

Set `lat`/`lon` here, or set HOME_LAT/HOME_LON in .env and omit them.

query.description: how many stops to poll, default 12

request.description:
What the device's firmware (or an app) consumes.

Rows are ordered **by line number** (numerically: 1, 1M, 90, 200, 906, ZC), not by arrival. Pass `sort=eta` for a time-ordered board.

`walk_minutes` and `leave_in_minutes` are still in the JSON even though the text view no longer prints them — the walk is what decides which buses make the board at all. Rows you can't reach in time are filtered out by default.

`stops_truncated` tells you whether `max_stops` stopped us polling everything in range, so a thin board can be read as 'we didn't look everywhere' rather than 'nothing runs'.

Each row carries **`realtime`** — true when STCP is actually tracking buses at that stop, false when it has fallen back to projecting from the timetable (`data_source` holds the raw upstream label). This is the field a display should key its colour off; the text view prints live times green.

request.description:
Fixed-width `text/plain`, ready to push straight at an LED matrix or a small display — no JSON parser needed on the device.

Columns: line, destination, minutes until arrival (`9m`). Ordered by line.

Curl it directly to see what the display would show.

`color=1` wraps live times in ANSI green — useful in a terminal, but off by default: a microcontroller driving an LED panel wants the `realtime` flag from `/board`, not escape codes it would have to strip.

Colour is applied after padding, so the fixed column width holds either way.
